description: We are from TIP, we just want to have a great experience and create a solution to a real-world problem using the NASA data.
summary:
Ani: An Extended Finite State Machine-Based Decision Support System for El Niño Dry-Season Crop Selection in Nueva Ecija is a decision support system that helps farmers choose suitable crops during the El Niño dry season in Guimba, Science City of Muñoz, and Bongabon, Nueva Ecija. It combines NASA weather and satellite data, soil information, crop water requirements, and local agricultural data to simulate past dry seasons and evaluate different crops. 

Ani recommends crops based on the farmer's available water, preferred priorities, and previous crops. It also provides information on water needs, potential crop failure, estimated income, and the reasons behind each recommendation. Through an Extended Finite State Machine, it provides clear and consistent decisions, including advice to delay planting when no crop is considered safe.

This project addresses the challenge of helping farmers adapt to changing climate conditions by turning scientific data into practical, location-specific guidance. It is important because it can help farmers reduce crop losses, manage limited water resources, protect their income, and make better planting decisions during El Niño.
details:
What it does:
Ani (“harvest”) is an offline-first mobile app (Flutter) that helps smallholder farmers in Nueva Ecija (Guimba, Science City of Muñoz and Bongabon) decide what to plant in an El Niño dry season. The farmer answers a few simple questions: their town, their last two crops, whether irrigation is available, the crops they won’t plant, and their priorities. Ani then suggests up to three crops, or a “Huwag munang magtanim” (Hold) message when no crop is safe. Once a crop is planted, Ani tracks it stage by stage and gives water and heat alerts. The app works in Filipino and English.

How it works:
A Python pipeline processes NASA POWER daily weather data (temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation, rainfall and root-zone soil wetness) for the three municipalities. From it we compute reference evapotranspiration (ET₀) and a soil-moisture proxy. We turn these into monthly z-scores and a dryness index, simulate each crop’s season with a finite-state machine, and tag past dry seasons as El Niño or La Niña using the NOAA CPC Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). SoilGrids soil properties feed the water-balance model. Crops are ranked by the farmer’s priorities using weighted-sum/TOPSIS scoring, based on past yields, prices and costs from PSA OpenSTAT and PSA costs and returns data. Results are bundled with the app, so advice works without internet. When a connection is available, the app fetches the latest NASA POWER data to update the home conditions card and the outlook. It also uses PAGASA heat index categories for its heat-safety advice.

Benefits and intended impact:
Farmers get clear, local, data-backed advice before committing seed, labor and money. This helps them avoid crop failure, save water, and plan around El Niño. The same design can grow to other regions and languages, and to farmers without smartphones (for example, SMS or voice).

Tools:
Python (data pipeline), NASA POWER API, Flutter/Dart (app), and git/GitHub.

What makes it creative:
Ani turns satellite-derived NASA data into a farmer’s plain-language decision rather than a dashboard. It is offline-first, bilingual, priority-aware, and willing to say “hold off” when no option is safe. It also tracks the crop after planting and gives heat-safety advice.

Factors we considered:
Our baseline period gives only a few El Niño seasons, so the app shows its uncertainty and confidence limits instead of hiding them. NASA POWER is a modeled dataset at a coarse grid, so it may not match conditions in a single field. Ani is advisory only, not a guarantee, and farmers should confirm with their Municipal Agriculture Office.
